title: Quantitative Gaussian limits of periodic O(N) models at and below the critical temperature
authors: Weiqi Jiang, Pengcheng Hou, Zhiyi Li
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14570v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We prove a volume-uniform Gaussian approximation for local spin coordinates in the zero-field nearest-neighbour $O(N)$ model on periodic boxes of side $M$ in $d\ge3$, at and below the critical temperature of the limiting spherical model. On a fixed spatial window, for sufficiently large $M,N$, the unnormalized $1$-Wasserstein error for the first $p\le N$ coordinates is at most $C\sqrt p (N^{-1/2}+s_M)$, where $s_M\to0$ is the spectral shift of the finite-volume mean spherical model. The estimate is uniform on compact ranges of positive directional couplings and inverse temperatures. The target has independent coordinate fields, each a scaled anisotropic Gaussian free field with an independent spatially constant Gaussian term below criticality.
  On a window containing a nearest-neighbour star (a site and its $d$ positive-direction neighbours), the error tends to zero as $M,N\to\infty$ exactly when $p=o(N)$ and $\sqrt p s_M\to0$. For any choice of periodic infinite-volume accumulation states, the error on any nonempty fixed window tends to zero as $N\to\infty$ exactly when $p=o(N)$. In $d\ge5$, when the inverse temperature exceeds its critical value by at least a fixed positive amount, the bound improves to $C(p/N+\sqrt p M^{-d})$. For fixed $p$, the sharp order is $N^{-1}+M^{-d}$ on star-containing windows and $N^{-1}$ on every nonempty fixed window in periodic accumulation states.

title: Rotor-driven piecewise cross polarization of wide quadrupolar lines: bath-contact pumping of vector and tensor order in dynamically polarized solids
authors: D. Keller, M. F. Hossain
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14575v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In a dynamically polarized solid with a common nuclear spin temperature, spin-1 $^{14}$N in ammonia sits at $P_N\simeq0.14$ when the protons are at $0.90$, and a deuteron in a proton-rich matrix at $P_D\simeq0.29$. Hartmann--Hahn cross polarization (CP) from the protons could raise either toward $P_H$, but the first-order quadrupole interaction spreads the $^{14}$N line over $5$~MHz at $5$~T, far beyond any single contact bandwidth. We develop the theory of CP into one transition of a quadrupolar spin-1, with slow sample rotation carrying each crystallite through a fixed-frequency contact window. A bath contact is an idempotent map on the populations of the contacted transition, so repeated or continuous contacts accumulate rather than cancel, and the hit-once and parity constraints that force stepped rotation for pulsed inversions do not arise. In the small-reservoir limit the population ratio across the contacted transition becomes $(1+P_H)/(1-P_H)$, giving $\Pzz=+0.88$ in one contact and $\Pzz\to-1.8$ in two from $P_H=0.9$, beyond the unitary bound $[-0.85,+0.65]$. Under continuous rotation, a window at the Pake horn reaches every bond for an axis perpendicular to the field, while a window in the clean pedestal region, needed for a definite sign of tensor order, reaches a fraction $\sin2\theta_c=0.943$ at the magic angle $54.74\degree$. Steady-state order is set by the contact rate against rotation-driven cross-branch relaxation, negligible for $^{14}$N. In the cubic limit one contact places the spin-1 at the proton temperature ($\Pzz=+0.85$), but only a resolved quadrupole splitting permits negative tensor order. The limiting resource is the proton spin lock, which must far exceed the $\simeq28$~kHz local field for a contact short compared with $T_{1\rho}$, unmeasured at $1$~K. Protocols are given for $^{14}$N in NH$_3$ and deuterons in NH$_2$D.

title: Rational layers in the low temperature expansion of the three-dimensional Ising model
authors: Ran Huang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14577v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A low-temperature expansion orders Ising droplets by wall area, but droplets with different transverse spans can occur at the same order. We instead organize the zero-field simple-cubic model by the excess above the minimum wall area compatible with two prescribed spans. We prove that every fixed excess layer, including all logarithmic cover corrections and Euler inversion, has a rational bivariate generating function with denominator factors restricted to 1 - x, 1 - y and 1 - x - y. The proof compresses repeated coordinate cuts into bounded decorations and assigns each unbounded interval to one monotone chain. A finite controller then enforces induced contacts and arbitrary cover-color reuse. We explicitly assemble the complete layers of excess zero through three over all widths, attributing their known geometric constituents to earlier polyomino enumeration. Exact lattice checks corroborate the formulas. A certified low-temperature comparison shows a modest hybrid accuracy gain at one sampling point and higher evaluation cost. The result establishes an exact layer structure; summation over unbounded excess remains a separate problem.

title: Circuit-aware protection against burst errors in lattice surgery
authors: Jaebum Kim
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14583v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Large-scale quantum computing will require logical operations protected against high-energy impacts that disturb many superconducting qubits at once. Gap engineering suppresses relaxation induced by these impacts, but protecting only a subset of qubits requires choosing where that protection is placed. During lattice surgery, measurements change as patches merge and split, exposing different ancillas and temporal boundaries to burst errors. Here we compare three static protection layouts for a simulated lattice-surgery CNOT, matching the numbers of protected ancillas and the X:Z check-type splits. At distance 9, protecting the check type measured during each merge reduces burst-induced excess risk by $38^{+6}_{-5}\%$ relative to a deep geometric band under correlated background matching, without giving the decoder the impact parameters. We attribute this difference to report errors at temporal boundaries and ancilla faults propagating to data, which interact to increase the excess risk of a shallow band. We also find that the typed layout reaches the shallow-band reference risk with an estimated $49^{+2}_{-14}$ fewer protected ancillas. At distance 13, the advantage is not resolved under oracle decoding, and a five-round burst cap reverses the shallow-band ordering. These results indicate how the measurements of a logical circuit can guide protection placement within the simulated decoder and burst-duration regimes tested here.

title: Controlled preparation and unconditional transport on a fluctuating quantum graph
authors: Xianbin Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14588v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Lieb--Robinson bounds limit the spread of quantum information, but do not establish that a prescribed input can be prepared and transmitted with appreciable probability. For quantum graphs with fluctuating edges, connecting spectral propagation to unconditional readout also requires control of graph coherence, finite boundaries, and preparation errors. We address this problem in a one-probe model on a prescribed square candidate lattice, combining a generalized Rokhsar--Kivelson parent, spectral reduction, adiabatic preparation, and local dynamical estimates. Assuming a supplied coherent graph ground state, we construct a finite-source wave packet and a hopping ramp that populate an isolated branch with strictly positive group velocity. We prove an unconditional arrival probability of at least $5/8$ in a specified receiver region of a sufficiently large finite open square. Explicit bounds on local joint-state and Hamiltonian errors retain a lower probability of $9/16$, without requiring global many-body state closeness or postselection on graph measurements. Exact arithmetic certificates and a separate small-system numerical diagnostic support the quantitative analysis. The construction provides a model-specific benchmark for transport and readout in fluctuating quantum networks, linking a propagation mechanism to an observable lower bound and identifying the local error budgets required to preserve it. It distinguishes suppression of unwanted influence from guaranteed signal delivery, a useful separation for quantum-network and emergent-geometry models. The resource estimates are conservative, graph-state supply is assumed, and the result does not establish background-free geometry or gravitational dynamics.

title: Optical trapping of neutral atoms via magnetic-dipole transitions
authors: E. Orellana-Paillaleo, N. Vera, P. Solano
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14607v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Optical trapping of neutral atoms is almost universally described as an electric-dipole (E1) effect. We show that the magnetic field of light, acting on a magnetic-dipole (M1) transition, can induce an ac Zeeman shift significantly larger than the ac Stark shift, thereby enabling magnetic trapping. We construct the M1 polarizability tensor and identify a critical detuning $\delta_c$, independent of optical power, below which the magnetic interaction dominates. We analyze suitable trapping parameters and possible loss mechanisms, particularly for the intraconfigurational transitions $^3H_6\rightarrow{}^3H_5$ of erbium at $1437.13$~nm and $^5I_8\rightarrow{}^5I_7$ of dysprosium at $2418.84$~nm. We propose two trapping configurations: a hybrid magnetic/electric optical tweezer and an optical lattice with separated magnetic and electric antinodes, producing state-dependent purely magnetic and purely electric trapping wells. Our results present optical magnetic fields as a suitable resource to expand the toolbox for atomic manipulation.

title: Probing Krylov Dynamics in Driven Many-Body Systems
authors: Andr\'as Grabarits, Adolfo del Campo
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14611v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Krylov complexity has become a central probe of operator growth, scrambling, and quantum chaos. Yet, a basic fact hinders its experimental study: laboratory quantum systems are routinely driven in time, whereas the Krylov construction assumes a fixed generator and breaks down once the Hamiltonian varies. Here, we solve the time-dependent many-body Krylov problem exactly and in closed form for scale- and rotation-invariant systems realized in current quantum-simulation and control platforms. We find exact relations that map the driven dynamics onto mutually orthogonal Krylov subspaces and yield a closed-form spread complexity, determined solely by the spectral properties of the initial Hamiltonian and the driving schedule. The construction extends to Liouville space and solves the time-dependent density-matrix Krylov problem, which makes the Krylov dynamics of initial thermal states experimentally accessible. In scale-invariant quantum gases, such as the driven Lieb-Liniger model, the Tonks-Girardeau gas, and the Calogero-Sutherland model, the complexity is set by the width of the atomic cloud and its rate of change, directly accessible via in situ and time-of-flight imaging. In rotation-invariant spin systems such as the Haldane-Shastry and central-spin models, it is governed by collective spin precession that can be probed and read out in trapped-ion, cavity-QED, and circuit-QED platforms.

title: Hidden universality of rare fluctuations and a central-limit structure at criticality
authors: Nikolaos G. Fytas, V\'ictor Mart\'in-Mayor, Attilio L. Stella, Gianluca Teza, Alexandros Vasilopoulos, David Yllanes
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14621v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The central limit theorem is among the most fundamental principles in the natural sciences, governing the fluctuations of sums of weakly correlated random variables through Gaussian statistics. At critical points, however, long-range correlations invalidate this paradigm, raising a fundamental question: does any general limit theorem survive at criticality? Although scale invariance has long been recognised as the defining feature of typical critical fluctuations, the behaviour of rare fluctuations has remained largely unexplored, as their extraordinarily small probabilities place them beyond the reach of conventional numerical methods. Recent theoretical advances suggest that universal asymptotic laws {may govern large deviations in systems at criticality}, yet direct numerical evidence has been lacking. Here we provide the first such evidence in the two-dimensional Ising universality class. Using large-scale Tethered Monte Carlo simulations, we probe order-parameter fluctuations with probabilities as small as $10^{-200}$ and show that, once normalised by their characteristic width, the far tails collapse onto a single asymptotic law shared by distinct microscopic models in the same universality class. This collapse is governed by a universal amplitude, whose numerical extraction is compatible with the conjectured exact result we derive from conformal field theory, and points towards a generalised central limit theorem for critical fluctuations.

title: Squeezed Light Generation by Cooper Pair Recombination in a Superconductor-Semiconductor Structure
authors: Sima Buchbinder, Avi Koriat, Alex Hayat
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14622v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We theoretically demonstrate squeezed light generation in a compact, electrically driven device utilizing the nonlinear light-matter interaction of Cooper-pair recombination in a hybrid superconductorsemiconductor structure. On the basis of second-order perturbation theory, we developed an effective Hamiltonian which incorporates the electronic component of the interaction as a photon coupling strength coefficient, enabling a model to describe the quadrature squeezing effect of Cooper-pair recombination on the photonic state. We find the squeezing strength to be proportional to the superconducting energy gap squared and device length, as well as increasing with applied voltage. For practical device length, materials and voltage bias, we calculated squeezing values comparable to those of existing squeezed light generation methods when operating below the critical temperature. This theoretically developed concept shows viability for electrically pumped squeezed light generation and can pave the way towards realization of squeezing in compact integrated structures.

title: Towards Distributed Quantum Computing: Quantum Gate Teleportation via Satellite-Distributed Entanglement under Atmospheric Depolarization
authors: Artur Czerwinski, Jakub J. Borkowski, Maciej Wi\'sniewski, Saeed Haddadi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14623v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate quantum gate teleportation as a primitive for satellite-enabled distributed quantum computing. In the considered architecture, a satellite distributes entangled photon pairs to two optical ground stations, which transfer the shared quantum resource to remote quantum processing units. This entanglement is then used to implement a nonlocal controlled-NOT gate between two circuit qubits located in different processors. We formulate the minimal four-qubit protocol, consisting of two network qubits that provide the entangled resource and two circuit qubits on which the distributed gate is performed. Atmospheric propagation effects in the gravitational field are modeled through an effective two-qubit depolarizing channel whose parameters depend on atmospheric and optical quantities, including the Fried parameter and receiver aperture. The performance of the protocol is quantified by the fidelity between the ideal CNOT output state and the state produced by noisy quantum gate teleportation. Our results show that the fidelity is governed by the quality of the distributed entanglement and depends jointly on atmospheric coherence, aperture size, and effective depolarization strength. These findings connect physical-layer modeling of satellite optical channels with gate-level performance in distributed quantum computing.

title: The memory cost of sequential quantum state preparation
authors: Jian Li, Patryk Lipka-Bartosik
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14652v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How much memory does a quantum device need to prepare systems one at a time? We address this question through the lens of quantum resource theories, which formalize physical restrictions on how the memory may interact with the stream of systems it processes. By comparing sequential with collective preparation, we show that under general assumptions both have the same asymptotic memory cost per output. Still, sequential preparation can require an unboundedly larger memory than collective one, and we investigate how this gap depends on the physical restrictions on the allowed interactions. For energy-conserving unitaries, we determine both optimal memory dimensions needed for preparing pure states from an energy eigenstate, and find that the extra memory required sequentially either remains bounded or grows logarithmically with the number of outputs. Under noisy operations, we reveal transformations for which one auxiliary qubit suffices for preparing arbitrarily many independent outputs collectively, while no memory of fixed dimension can deliver them sequentially. Finally, for sequential protocols that repeat a fixed interaction, we show that a $d$-dimensional memory that succeeds for $d^2$ rounds will succeed forever, and that such a sequential preparation is equivalent to quantum catalysis.

title: Quantum synchronization in XX chains under relaxation
authors: K\"ubra S\"umer, Ege Yi\u{g}it Ald{\i}rmaz, Steve Campbell, Bar{\i}\c{s} \c{C}akmak, G\"oktu\u{g} Karpat
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14657v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study stable synchronization in qubit XX chains with site-dependent frequencies and exchange couplings under multi-local amplitude damping noise, extending the uniform-chain results of B. \c{C}akmak et al., [Phys. Rev. A 114, L030202 2026] in several directions. We establish that the dark-mode energies are precisely the eigenvalues shared by all undamped segments separated by the damped sites. Generic stable synchronization of the edge qubits occurs if and only if these segments share exactly one eigenvalue and this eigenvalue is nonzero, in which case every qubit on the support of the corresponding dark mode is synchronized with locking constants independent of the initial preparation. This spectral matching condition identifies the Hamiltonian parameters that support synchronization, while the couplings to the damped sites control the relative oscillation amplitudes. We present analytical examples which show how inhomogeneity can create synchronization absent in uniform chains and turn preparation-dependent locking into generic synchronization. We also calculate the asymptotic pairwise concurrence and prove that, in the single-dark-mode regime, every pair participating in synchronized oscillations remains entangled with a nonzero, constant concurrence.

title: Emergent Anyons in a Weakly Interacting Gauged Chern Insulator
authors: Sven Bachmann, Leonardo Goller, Marcello Porta
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14658v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We derive a microscopic relation between the many-body Chern number $C$ of the fermionic ground state and the braiding of fluxes in $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ gauge theory coupled to matter: under a spectral gap condition, dressed flux loops obey $W_2W_1=e^{i\frac{\pi}{2}C}W_1W_2$ on the ground-state sector. We realize $C=1$ by gauging charge parity in a weakly interacting Qi-Wu-Zhang insulator. Reflection positivity and chessboard estimates show that flux defects are massive, which yields a gapped, topologically ordered phase with four locally indistinguishable ground states.

title: AI-assisted search for self-compressing gigawatt subcycle field waveforms
authors: Aleksei M. Zheltikov, Youchan Park, Petr Zhokhov, Julia M. Mikhailova
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14672v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We explore the physics behind pulse self-compression to high-power subcycle field waveforms and search for the optimal regimes of such compression over the parameter space as laid out by multimode nonlinear dynamics of ultrashort laser pulses in gas-filled hollow fibers. With the pertinent physical criteria for pulse contrast and no pulse breakup formalized as operational stopping rules, a radical speedup of such search is achieved by delegating its tedious preliminary stages to generative pretrained transformer models. The precise adjustment of self-compression dynamics vis-a-vis the desired compressed pulse output is, however, not yet delegable to AI agents, as the criteria for such search are still largely subjective, operating with fine aspects of subcycle field structure, not yet formalizable as clear search-stopping instructions. An ultimate precision in such subcycle field engineering is attainable via a management of field-phase-sensitive nonlinear processes, enabling pulse self-compression to high-power subcycle field waveforms and opening paths toward fiber-optic attosecond lightwave engineering.

title: Faithful filtering of constrained quantum records: Local limits and collective advantage from loops
authors: Qingtian Miao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14695v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weak probes can record whether neighboring spins are aligned without revealing their common orientation. Reading the probes can then herald a projection of an unknown spin state onto the aligned subspace that preserves every coherence within it. We ask how often this projection succeeds when the probes are read separately or jointly. For binary pure product records and zero false positives, we derive the exact optimum over all separable measurements, and hence over all local operations and classical communication. It is the probability that one-sided local witnesses exclude every alternative, and simultaneous local measurements attain it. Joint readout can do better by accepting coherent combinations of ambiguous outcomes in which the alternatives cancel. For pairwise parity records on a connected simple graph, it beats every local strategy exactly when the graph has a loop, at all record overlaps strictly between zero and one. For general binary linear records, the condition is an irreducible dependency among at least three records. The advantage lowers the leading power of the efficiency at weak recording. On a triangle the efficiency becomes linear rather than quadratic in the witness probability, and a three-pulse coherent-light receiver captures this gain with a single click. Extensions treat targets spanning several patterns and a noisy comparison at a common output fidelity.

title: Force-Dependent Change of Structural Behavior Upon Pulling a Grafted Flexible Polymer
authors: J. Matthew Smith, Michael Bachmann
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14720v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Manipulating polymer chains by means of experimental instruments such as optical tweezers has helped understand better the effects of molecular forces in macromolecular structures. In this study, we simulate the influence of a pulling force on structural phases of a coarse-grained model for flexible polymers using generalized-ensemble Monte Carlo methodologies. The recently introduced microcanonical inflection-point analysis method is employed to identify and classify structural phases of the system. Specific order parameters help characterize the transition behavior in response to the present pulling force. We show that, upon increasing the pulling strength, the coil-globule transition turns from second to first order, then merges with the liquid-solid transition. An intermediate phase, separating the coil and globule phases, is identified for certain force strengths. Clear evidence of the Gough-Joule effect is found as well. Transitions do not occur at all if the pulling force exceeds a certain threshold value.

title: A New Framework for Quantum Reinforcement Learning
authors: Alireza Tavakoli, Mohsen Heidari
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14731v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) has emerged as a promising approach for controlling quantum systems and accelerating learning tasks with quantum resources. However, most existing QRL formulations still retain a classical reinforcement learning interface: states and actions are often encoded in computational bases and rewards are extracted through measurements. This interface is restrictive for genuinely quantum environments: choosing a measurement can discard entanglement information, while repeated intermediate measurements collapse the evolving state and require costly re-preparation. This motivates a fully QRL framework in which the agent, environment, rewards, and return accumulation are all quantum. In this paper, we take a step toward this goal and introduce a new QRL framework in which both the policy and the environment are modeled by conditional quantum channels. We then propose a quantum policy-gradient algorithm for parameterized conditional quantum channels with a trainable control basis. We also derive finite- and infinite-horizon gradient estimators using a new parameter-shift rule. This rule is needed because policy parameters are shared across repeated interaction blocks and the infinite-horizon objective is not a finite circuit; rather than shifting every occurrence and evaluating the whole trajectory, our estimator shifts only one sampled policy block. Sampling this block from a geometric distribution yields an unbiased gradient estimator under bounded rewards. Finally, we establish convergence of the resulting stochastic gradient-ascent procedure to stationary points under standard smoothness and step-size assumptions.

title: Making Poisson {\sigma} again - an \'etude on groupoidal gauging, anomalies, gerbes, and defects
authors: Rafa{\l} R. Suszek
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14784v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Poisson $\sigma$-model (PSM) over a closed worldsheet $\Sigma$ is reinterpreted as a theory of connections on a trivial principaloid bundle $P_0 = \Sigma \times G \to \Sigma$ with the symplectic structure groupoid $(G,\omega)$ integrating the Poisson target $(M,\Pi)$, and that of sections of the shadow bundle $F_0 = \Sigma \times M \to \Sigma$ - as defined in 2503.09886 [math.DG]. The flat directions of the PSM are explained as linearisations of automorphisms of $P_0$, modelled on maps from $\Sigma$ into the group of lagrangean bisections of $G$, which induce Poisson automorphisms of $(M,\Pi)$. The gauge anomaly of the ensuing field theory is derived and demonstrated to vanish for prequantisable $\omega$. A general anomaly-cancellation mechanism is proposed, which couples the bare model - rewritten as the holonomy of a connection-dependent trivial gerbe on $F_0$ - to a background gerbe over $M$ endowed with a $G$-equivariant structure. The coupling takes the form of the tensor product of the two gerbes and the extended PSM is defined as the holonomy of the product gerbe. An essential generalisation of the theory is then proposed - to shadows $F$ of principaloid bundles $P$ of arbitrary topology, in keeping with the interpretation of the gauging as descent to the orbistack $M//G$. The generalisation uses local product gerbes depending on local connections over trivialisations of $F$. The $G$-equivariant structure is proven to ensure a 2-stacky descent of the local gerbes to a global one over $F$. Its holonomy is taken as the definition of the generalised PSM. A cohomological discussion of obstructions against the descent is provided. Finally, a reformulation of the generalised PSM as a field theory with a topological gauge-symmetry defect is given, in which the $G$-equivariant structure is employed - alongside the transition cocycle of $P$ - as the datum of the defect.

title: Bounding Freedom of Choice via Causal Network Embeddings
authors: George Moreno, Emanuele Polino, Giovanni Rodari, Davide Poderini, Askery Canabarro, Elie Wolfe, Robert W. Spekkens, Fabio Sciarrino, Rafael Chaves
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14791v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Standard Bell inequalities rely on measurement independence, the assumption that measurement settings are perfectly decoupled from the source of correlations. We demonstrate that embedding Bell scenarios into larger causal networks naturally overcomes this limitation. This embedding yields experimentally accessible lower and upper bounds on measurement dependence, the incompatibility of which certifies nonclassicality directly from data, without assuming a priori freedom of choice. We formulate a general linear-programming framework to systematically derive these measurement-dependence consistency (MDC) Bell inequalities. By bypassing standard non-convexity hurdles, this approach significantly outperforms existing techniques in computational simplicity and noise robustness. Finally, we reveal that genuine quantum nonlocality can be certified even for correlations exceeding the Tsirelson bound, and demonstrate our method's broad applicability to multi-outcome and multipartite Bell tests.

title: Plasma simulations with adaptive mesh and algorithm refinement
authors: Vladimir I. Kolobov, Robert R. Arslanbekov
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14820v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Adaptive Mesh and Algorithm Refinement (AMAR) combines adaptive Cartesian meshes with automatic selection of kinetic or fluid solvers. It was introduced for rarefied gas dynamics and later extended to gas mixtures, particle and lattice-Boltzmann solvers, computational electromagnetics, and multi-phase flows. In weakly ionized plasmas, the species differ by orders of magnitude in mass, velocity, and time scale. This paper describes PAMAR, a plasma extension of AMAR in which electrons, ions, neutral species, and fields can have independent adaptive-mesh solvers, each with its own phase-space dimensionality, refinement criteria, and time step, coupled through a field solver in one executable built on the Basilisk framework. We present two demonstrations. A transient capacitively coupled plasma in argon is simulated with two-stream kinetic solvers for electrons and ions on independent adaptive quadtrees in $(x,v)$. The simulations resolve three electron groups and the time scales of electron and ion kinetics without statistical noise, at a cost between particle-in-cell simulations and fast kinetic models. A sphere at floating potential in a collisionless or weakly collisional plasma is computed with octree solvers in $(r,v,\mu)$ for both species and compared with an exact method-of-characteristics solution. Per-species meshes resolve the cold ions at a tenth of the uniform-mesh cost. Both demonstrations also select the model cell by cell. In the capacitive discharge, a hybrid ion solver is kinetic in the sheaths and fluid in the bulk. Around the sphere, a hybrid electron solver confines the kinetic solver to the loss-cone layer and uses a Fokker-Planck model in position and total energy elsewhere. It conserves particles exactly across the interface and uses 1.6 to 5.3 times fewer cells. We discuss the next steps toward parallel, implicit simulations of higher-dimensional problems.

title: Quantum Telatar formula: fading quantum capacity of Haar-random multimode attenuators
authors: Eric Culf, Victor V. Albert
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14822v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Cellular communication is done over an imperfectly predictable multimode environment, where the sender only knows about the distribution of possible intermode coupling and scattering a signal faces. It may thus seem surprising that such communication is efficient. Telatar proved that the sender's lack of exact knowledge about the channel, on average, does not significantly hinder multimode communication. As the number $N$ of modes increases at fixed signal-to-noise ratio, the average capacity of a classical multimode fading channel grows linearly in $N$, like that of $N$ decoupled single-mode channels. We study the quantum analogue in a Haar-random passive bosonic network and prove a similar scaling for unassisted quantum information transmission. Suppose that the sender drives a fixed fraction of the input modes and the receiver collects more than half of the output modes. Then the quantum capacity of such channels at zero temperature grows linearly with the number of modes at fixed photon number per mode, just like the classical capacity grows with the number of antennas. At nonzero temperature, the Haar-averaged coherent information of the isotropic thermal input bounds the capacity from below, and its value per mode converges to an integral against Wachter's law. We numerically identify positive achievable rates in models motivated by cryogenic microwave networks and room-temperature multimode fibers.

title: Locating Debunkers for Rumor Mitigation in Directed Networks
authors: Kasra Ghorbani, Xinshan Jiao, Tao Zhou
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14825v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rumors can spread widely through social networks, making the selection of a limited number of debunkers to disseminate corrective information important. Existing centrality-based methods only consider the individual influence of a node on spreading processes. Those individually influential nodes often have heavily overlapping influence ranges, resulting in a limited number of users they can cover. To address this problem, we propose the so-called Hybrid Marginal Influence (HMI) framework, which combines node centrality with additional audience coverage provided by each candidate and adaptively balances these two factors through a greedy selection procedure. We further develop the Debunker-Augmented SIR (DA-SIR) model for the propagation of rumors and corrective information. Experiments on ten real-world directed networks show that HMI generally selects debunkers with broader audience coverage than conventional centrality-based methods, accompanied by a lower final cumulative fraction of users who repost the rumor.

title: High-directivity pulsed beams for effective power and information transfer
authors: Richard W. Ziolkowski
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14860v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A vector spherical wave expansion (VSWE) is used to engineer an elemental multipole source whose radiated field is a superdirective, extremely unidirectional (SDEU) needle beam. It is proved analytically and confirmed numerically that the element attains Harrington's normal-directivity value along its beam axis. Its radiated field is linearly polarized with an azimuthally symmetric magnitude; its back lobe vanishes identically in the far field. The unidirectional behavior is quantified at any finite far-field radius by a closed-form front-to-back ratio, obtained from an exact per-degree cancellation of the electric and magnetic multipole contributions in the backward direction. Uniform circular arrays (UCAs) of these elements inherit the SDEU behavior. Driving the arrays with zero-area pulses (ZAPs) transfers the frequency-domain performance intact into the time domain. It is shown that whether the radiated energy beam is narrower or wider than the corresponding intensity beam is decided by a single property of the radiated waveform, not by the size of the radiating aperture. A simple single-cycle ZAP is used to quantify the performance of the UCAs; its energy beam is the narrower one. The same criterion is shown to govern the focal spot of near-field-focused pulse-driven arrays. A custom-designed intensity-enhancement (IE) ZAP is introduced that raises the focal intensity by almost 200-fold over a narrow-band reference while producing a focal spot more than ten times smaller in both the axial and transverse directions, deeply subwavelength with respect to its own effective wavelength. It is demonstrated that these stunning IE results are produced simply with an array of pulse-excited Huygens dipole sources. These results identify the pulse shape, rather than the aperture, as the design variable that governs localized electromagnetic energy and information delivery.

title: Optimal Driving between Nonequilibrium Steady States under a Dissipation Budget
authors: Keisuke Sugie, Dimitri Loutchko, Tetsuya J. Kobayashi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14891v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Driving between nonequilibrium steady states incurs two thermodynamic costs: excess entropy production (EP) resulting from changing control parameters, and housekeeping EP required to sustain steady currents. Conventional fixed-duration optimization minimizes the former while neglecting the latter. Here, we instead optimize excess EP over both the protocol and its duration subject to a fixed leading order of housekeeping-EP budget, thereby minimizing total EP for that budget constraint. In the slow-driving regime, accumulated housekeeping EP acts as an entropic time, mapping the problem to a geodesic optimization under a friction metric weighted by the steady-state EP rate. This resource-based geometry determines optimal paths and schedules for systems that continue to dissipate even in steady states, establishing an intrinsic trade-off between housekeeping and excess EPs. Near equilibrium, this framework further yields geometric lower bounds on total EP, attained with equipartition at the optimal budget given by a modified thermodynamic length. Numerical simulations of a three-state model for an ATP-driven calcium pump reveal distinct optimal protocols compared to fixed-duration driving, confirming the total-EP bounds.

title: Evaluating Quantum Circuit Protection Methods After Compilation: An Empirical Comparison
authors: Ing Muyleang, Leanghok Hour, Youngsun Han
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14919v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum cloud providers can read the circuits they receive and their outputs, yet methods for hiding a circuit are usually evaluated on the circuit as written, before compilation optimises it. We compare three ObfusQate schemes (inverse, composite and delayed gates), ECQCO and Q-MaskCut under one protocol that compiles every protected circuit at optimisation level 3 before measuring it; the goal is to keep the provider from learning the user's algorithm and answer. Q-MaskCut is one example combination of existing techniques: a one-time-pad key, decoy wires, circuit cutting with a random rotation pair across each cut, and Pauli twirling with dynamical-decoupling masking after compilation. We simulate 11 circuits of 3 to 19 qubits without noise and on two noise models, measure the compiled structure and execution time of 23 circuits of 3 to 127 qubits, and test whether the structural disguise survives a second compilation by the provider. Composite and delayed gates lose most of their structural disguise in compilation and leave the output readable; inverse gates keep a high normalised graph edit distance (normGED) only by making execution 7 to 112 times longer; ECQCO's output could not be decoded with the implementation provided by its authors. Q-MaskCut hides the output (mean total variation distance without the key 0.94), and without noise, with exact fragment probabilities, it decodes exactly. Its compiled normGED of 0.88 comes mostly from the masking, which a second compilation removes, leaving 0.42 from the key, decoys and padlocks. With noise, its fidelity is comparable to the original's; it needs 7 to 91 fragment variants per circuit in the simulations (7 to 61 in a run on ibm_marrakesh) and a classical reconstruction. Protection should therefore be evaluated on the compiled circuit and again after the provider recompiles it.

title: Quantum CSS codes: Decoder-aware multiobjective design and bound-certified selection
authors: Jiapei Zhuang, Yaocheng Chen, Xingyao Wu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14923v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes trade decoding reliability against the resources needed to measure their checks. We formulate Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) code design at fixed encoding resources as a decoder-aware multiobjective problem. The objectives are failure probability under sector-wise degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding and check weight, the minimum total weight of an independent pure-type generator basis. For independent bit- and phase-flip noise with perfect syndrome extraction, deterministic truncation bounds support selection under a failure-rate constraint. At a per-sector error probability of 0.01, the bounds certify that a code encoding two logical qubits into 40 physical qubits meets a failure-rate target of 0.001 at check weight 139. The lower bound of every cheaper candidate in the corresponding (40,2) main menu exceeds this target. In paired searches sharing one annealing kernel and equal query budgets, decoder-aware guidance gives significantly higher mean final hypervolume than distance guidance in all eight tested configurations under the reported Holm correction. Against distance-multiplicity guidance, five configurations show significant gains and three do not, including one with a negative mean difference. All arms are scored in common truncated-reliability and normalized-check-weight coordinates. The framework connects reliability-check-weight trade-offs to bound-certified selection within evaluated CSS pools.

title: CSS Circuits: useful quantum circuits that can be simulated with $O(1)$ cost per gate
authors: Craig Gidney, Cody Jones
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14944v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: "CSS circuits" are quantum circuits generated by $X$, $Z$, $M_X$, $M_Z$, and CNOT gates. Although CSS circuits are extremely restrictive, they can implement important quantum protocols like teleportation, error correction, and entanglement purification.
  We present a simple CSS circuit simulator that uses $O(1)$ work per gate. The simulator corresponds to a local hidden variable model, so we use Bell inequalities to prove the simulator can't also support Hadamard gates, CZ gates, or S gates. We note that CSS circuits appear ideal for benchmarking quantum error correction in the presence of atom loss errors.

title: Distilling an atomistic foundation model is all you need for large-scale molecular dynamics of semiconductor interfaces
authors: Feiyu Zhou, Wei Qiu, Fei Shuang, Yilun Liu, Shengying Yue, Penghua Ying
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14948v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: State-of-the-art atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable energy and force predictions, but their direct deployment in large-scale molecular dynamics remains computationally costly. Here we examine whether their knowledge can be distilled into compact potentials while retaining the physical responses of heterogeneous semiconductor interfaces. From 128 pretrained models spanning 22 model families, we select a fixed EquiformerV3 teacher and train atomic cluster expansion (ACE) and neuroevolution potential (NEP) students without target-specific teacher fine-tuning, with both simulation speed and accessible system size improved by several orders of magnitude relative to the teacher model. Matched training configurations and architectures enable direct comparisons with students trained on density-functional-theory (DFT) reference labels. For 79,920-atom BAs/GaN interfaces, direct distillation preserves termination-dependent thermal conductance and dominant spectral features, with conductance differing by at most 6.6% from DFT-trained counterparts. In 29,792-atom Cu/diamond specimens loaded at 500 K, tensile strength and loading work differ by 2.8% and 1.5%, respectively. Exploratory SiC/a-C/SiC simulations retain the principal thermal bottleneck and the direction of the annealing response. Furthermore, a four-model committee retrieves 42-56% of the highest-error teacher configurations with a 10% selection budget and improves high-error force fitting, but does not consistently improve downstream properties. These findings demonstrate that direct distillation can preserve key interfacial thermal and mechanical responses in compact interatomic potentials, opening a path towards large-scale, high-throughput simulations of heterogeneous interfaces.

title: Local enhancement of finite-strength code preparation: recoverability and Wilson coherence
authors: Tong Xu, Yuanchen Zhao, Dong E. Liu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14967v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Stabilizer measurements provide a direct route to preparing quantum error-correcting codes and long-range entangled states. In realistic implementations, however, finite measurement strength can coherently deform the encoding map away from the projective limit. Certain nonlocal signatures associated with long-range order can survive such a deformation, but this alone does not guarantee that the resulting state protects encoded quantum information. We show that, at fixed strength, local logical leakage obstructs asymptotically faithful recovery; along logical operators' supports, its accumulation forces the relevant measurement strength to grow logarithmically with code distance. We then prove that this obstruction can be removed locally: for fixed toric registers under sufficiently weak local-stochastic errors, enhancing only a vanishing fraction of checks near selected logical supports restores recovery while the bulk remains at finite measurement strength. With recoverability restored, we prove a further dimensional distinction in logical operations. In the strict three-dimensional deconfined phase, suitable enhanced tubes restore the equivalence of macroscopically separated representatives, so either representative asymptotically implements the same controlled logical action on a fixed encoding. In two dimensions, recoverability alone does not restore this equivalence: the representatives can remain inequivalent even when both associated encodings are recoverable.

title: From optimization to construction: Expanding quantum measurement designs
authors: Taotao Zhao, Qianjun Yao, Mengdi Sun, He Li
abstract:
arXiv:2611.14986v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Estimating molecular energies on quantum computers requires repeated measurements of many Pauli terms, making sampling a major resource cost. Measurement design chooses which compatible terms are measured together and allocates a finite shot budget among bases to minimize the variance of an energy estimator. We introduce variance-guided measurement group construction (VGMC), which reduces variance beyond optimization on existing measurement bases by changing which Hamiltonian terms share measurement shots. After including every Hamiltonian term measurable in each existing basis, we jointly optimize estimator coefficients and shot allocations to separate inefficient use of these measurements from limitations of their measurement combinations. We compare a candidate's benefit with the cost of withdrawing shots from existing bases, and use the resulting scores to guide greedy construction of qubit-wise commuting groups followed by joint re-optimization. With exact covariances, VGMC outperformed the state-of-the-art measurement design methods across the molecular benchmarks where it introduced additional measurement bases, achieving variance reductions of 18.19%-23.38%. The gains persisted with approximate covariances, and simulations with finite shots indicated lower estimated shot requirements near chemical accuracy. These results show that optimizing how measurements are combined can also guide which terms are measured together, offering a route to reducing the sampling overhead of variational quantum simulation while retaining local measurements on current and near-term devices.

title: QSim-Arena: an evolving developer for quantum simulation advantage
authors: Jue Xu, Yue Wang, Qi Zhao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15000v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Where practical advantage emerges in quantum dynamics simulation remains a central debate in quantum computing. Claimed advantages can be rapidly narrowed or overturned by stronger classical methods, while progress on both sides can outpace the journal publication cycle. We present QSim-Arena, a research framework in which AI agents combine a closed loop of verification and benchmarking with open exploration. Hamiltonians, initial states and accuracy targets for evolved states or observable expectation values provide explicit specifications for evaluating simulation methods. Agents translate published techniques into executable components, reproduce reported results and benchmark their performance across diverse Hamiltonian families. Competing classical methods are implemented and independently crosschecked, providing credible baselines for end-to-end quantum resource estimates based on rigorous error bounds and empirical calibration. Alongside this closed loop, agents recombine classical simulation techniques and co-design fault-tolerant quantum circuits using knowledge extracted from the literature. Initial applications improve baseline resource estimates through the integration of established techniques. QSim-Arena thus treats quantum advantage assessment as an evolving, reproducible research process that can respond to advances in algorithms, error analysis and hardware.

title: A Field-Deployable 2U Ultra-Stable Laser with Sub-Hertz Linewidth Based on Optoelectronic Oscillator Locking
authors: Dongdong Jiao, Linbo Zhang, Xue Deng, Jing Gao, Yue Gao, Mengfan Wu, Qi Zang, Guanjun Xu, Tao Liu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15005v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Compact, high-performance ultra-stable lasers that can operate outside the laboratory remain a long-standing goal. Here we report, to our knowledge, the most compact field-deployable ultra-stable laser, packaged in a standard 2U rack chassis. It is stabilized to a 50 mm-long, 19 mL optical reference cavity with low vibration sensitivity by optoelectronic oscillator (OEO) locking, an approach particularly suited to compact, transportable systems. The laser delivers an integrated linewidth of about 0.42 Hz and a fractional frequency stability of about 5E-15 at 1 s averaging time (about 2.2E-15 at 0.4 s). Measured phase noise approaches the cavity thermal-noise limit below 100 Hz and the theoretical OEO-locking limit from 100 Hz to 100 kHz. The system volume is roughly one quarter of the volume of previously reported integrated, transportable ultra-stable lasers of comparable performance, making it well suited for field applications in time-frequency metrology, quantum technologies, and environmental sensing.

title: Time- and Photon-Optimal Paths for the Preparation and Logical Flip of Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill States
authors: Aidan Curtis, Juan S. Salcedo-Gallo, Sergei Leonov, Kevin Limanta, Peter Chin, Salil Bedkihal, Mattias Fitzpatrick
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15018v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states are highly non-Gaussian, making their control challenging, particularly in the presence of photon loss. Here, we use the brachistochrone, the fastest path at bounded speed, to construct ideal nonlinear Hamiltonians for state preparation and logical gates, and compare it with the photon-optimal path. We find that the two paths nearly coincide for state preparation but differ markedly for logical operations, namely the brachistochrone preserves the encoded qubit during a bit flip, whereas the photon-optimal path flips a known state through the vacuum. We then introduce the tangential capacity to quantify how effectively gate sets track these paths. Using this analysis, we find that conditional squeezing achieves the highest capacity, preparing GKP states in 824 ns with a fidelity of 0.99 and a minimum closeness to the path of 0.90, compared with 0.98 and 0.51 for conditional displacements and 0.83 and 0.19 for SNAP gates.

title: Reducing TLS Losses in Superconducting Circuits Using Solid Neon
authors: A. Palmer, K. Matkovic, P. Russell, E. Helgemo, L. Delventhal, Y. Ashlea Alava, K. Zuo, S. N. Coppersmith, M. C. Cassidy
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15021v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Two level systems (TLSs) are a major source of loss in superconducting devices, limiting the performance of qubits, detectors, and resonators. These defects arise from a range of sources, including surface oxides, crystal defects, as well as fabrication residues which are often difficult to remove. Using NbTiN coplanar waveguide resonators, we show that depositing and subsequently removing a solid neon film can significantly improve device performance. Analysis of the temperature and power dependence indicates that this enhancement arises from reduced TLS dissipation, which we attribute to the redistribution and removal of surface contaminants during neon deposition and evaporation. Atomic force microscopy images of contaminated hexagonal boron nitride flakes before and after neon exposure show that neon treatment can redistribute and remove surface residues. These results demonstrate a simple, non-destructive approach for mitigating TLS losses in superconducting devices and other sensitive materials that cannot withstand aggressive cleaning processes.

title: High-precision measurement of level leakage via intelligent coherent control
authors: Ting Wang, Hang Xu, Shi-Qiang Qiao, Xue-Ke Song, Haipeng Cao, Zhao-Feng Su, Liu Ye, Dong Wang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15031v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Level leakage constitutes a dominant error source in quantum state control and necessitates accurate characterization for large-scale quantum computing. Quantum sensing provides a viable route for high-precision estimation of level leakage, but its sensitivity can be limited by non-unitary leakage dynamics and interference between the free Hamiltonian and signal generator. This work proposes a reinforcement learning-based quantum sensing algorithm for Hermitian three-level and effective dissipative two-level systems. The algorithm adopts an experimentally feasible pulse-parameter modulation strategy, enabling high-precision and reliable measurement under the specified control and measurement protocol. In both models, DQN-discovered pulse sequences enhance the measurement-model-specific sensing precision, while joint phase--detuning modulation further improves the performance and yields a CFI close to the corresponding QFI.

title: Sensing frequencies at the discrete Grover-Heisenberg limit using a single qubit
authors: Boyang Chen, Andrea Coladangelo, Jerry Li, Haocheng Zhang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15057v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We consider a fundamental quantum sensing task: detecting weak oscillating fields with unknown strength and frequency. Recent work by Allen et al. established a fundamental lower bound on the required sensing time, which they named the "Grover-Heisenberg limit", and gave a protocol attaining this limit. The protocol relies on auxiliary qubits, which are used to run Grover's algorithm as a subroutine, leaving open the question of whether a single sensing qubit can achieve the same scaling.
  We show that a single qubit suffices for a discrete version of this problem, in which the signal strength is known and the frequency belongs to an arbitrary, but known, finite set of candidate frequencies. Our protocol's sensing time grows only as the square root of the number of candidate frequencies. We prove that this square-root dependence, which we refer to as the "discrete Grover-Heisenberg limit", is optimal in the worst case.

title: Scalable Compilation of Resource-Efficient Tapers for High-Confidence Quantum Phase Estimation
authors: David Raveh, Andrew Sornborger, Yi\u{g}it Suba\c{s}\i, Lukasz Cincio
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15076v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum phase estimation is a key component of many quantum algorithms. Recently, high-confidence, tapered QPE (tQPE) has been introduced, significantly reducing the number of ancilla qubits necessary for a given failure probability, $\epsilon$. We consider tQPE with $p = l+m$ ancillas, where $l$ represents the number of ancillas necessary to estimate a phase to a given resolution and $m$ represents the number of ''confidence'' qubits added to ensure a desired success probability. With tQPE the failure probability decays double exponentially in $m$, implying that only a few confidence qubits suffice for virtually any problem of interest. A key challenge for tQPE is the construction of the quantum circuit for preparing the taper state on the ancilla register. Here, we develop scalable tensor network methods (previous work was limited to ($l + m = 24$)) giving highly optimized state preparation circuits for optimally concentrated DPSS (Slepian) tapers. We provide an accompanying database of resource-efficient state preparation circuits for $l = 1, \dots, 50$ and $m = 1, \dots, 4$. Our circuits are shallow enough for a demonstration on near-term devices for small values of $l$. We run tQPE circuits for a 1-qubit system initialized in the ground state on Quantinuum's H2-2 quantum computer, demonstrating a $3\times$ to $18\times$ reduction in failure probability for $l=1,\ldots,10$ on a noisy device.

title: A Diffusive T-Matrix Unifying the Electric and Magnetic Polarizability Tensors in Conducting Layered Media
authors: Fraser Williams, Dhammika Jayalath, Clinton Fookes, Ajay Pandey
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15090v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Electromagnetic induction is used to detect and classify buried and submerged objects, such as unexploded ordnance in soil and on the seabed. A small object is commonly described by its magnetic polarizability tensor (MPT), which is independent of its position and of the sensor. The MPT assumes that the surrounding medium does not conduct. In seawater at extremely low frequency, or in clay at kilohertz frequencies, this assumption fails at depths comparable to the skin depth. The object then also diverts the current induced in the medium, a galvanic response that the MPT omits. We describe the object instead by its transition matrix (T-matrix), which keeps the independence from position and sensor and includes both responses. It is computed once per medium and frequency from a single finite element problem, for any shape and materials. Its inductive block reduces to the MPT when the medium conducts weakly, and its galvanic block reduces to the electric polarizability tensor in the static limit. We test the model against full finite element solutions for a conducting box, non-magnetic and permeable, in a layered sea and in clay over bedrock. Two orders beyond the dipole, it is accurate to within 1.4% over two decades of frequency and for sizes up to 0.7 of the depth, whereas the error of the MPT carried into the conducting medium reaches 91%. Blocks coupling the two responses, contained in neither tensor, contribute up to 13%.

title: One molecule, many outputs; many molecules, one output: exact diagnostics for atom-level compositional quantum encoders
authors: Gautami Sanjay Naik, Ashwanth Krishnan
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15092v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum natural language processing (QNLP) turns the grammar of a sentence into a tensor network and then into a quantum circuit with trainable angles. We build such a model for molecules: each heavy atom is a word with one wire per bond, and each bond is a ``cup'' joining two wires, so the circuit's wiring is the molecular graph. We work out exactly what these circuits keep. With the typed angle sharing of lambeq, the circuits separate every isomer pair we tested. Yet for isomers that simpler sharing confuses, the output states stay almost the same, before and after training. On 7 Tox21 pairs and 1,988 MOSES pairs, nearly all the difference lies in how often the measurements succeed, which a standard readout ignores. Simpler sharing, by element and bond type, shows why: the output then depends only on a graph whose vertices are the bonds. This explains all but one of the identical-output pairs we certify, including 1.19\% of 232{,}191 MOSES molecules, and for alkyl side chains it reduces to a tree shape that tells chains apart up to 15 atoms but not from 16. On small pairs, this circuit and the 1-WL graph test each separate pairs the other misses. We also show that SMILES writing order can change the output, that a run succeeds with probability at most $2^{-n}$ for $n$ bonds, and that a cup-free design avoids this cost. No circuit beats a simple atom-count model on Tox21, and we claim no quantum advantage.

title: An Architecture for Real-Time Quantum Error Correction with Neutral Atoms
authors: X. Wang, Y. Jing, Z. Yu, S. Wang, D. Niu, Y. Liu, T. Xiao, A. Yang, J. Han, Y. Wu, X. Lv
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15104v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The latency of quantum measurement and classical decoding constrains the execution of adaptive fault-tolerant circuits. In neutral-atom processors, this requirement couples spatially resolved fluorescence detection to classical inference. Here we implement cascaded readout and decoding in a heterogeneous architecture that overlaps acquisition and processing at two spatial scales. Field-programmable gate arrays process camera rows as they arrive, while graphics processors decode an acquired logical block during acquisition of the next. This heterogeneous architecture offers flexibility in the choice of error-correcting codes and decoding algorithms. Direct communication preserves microsecond-scale transfer times for kilobyte payloads and supports interchangeable decoding algorithms. Hardware characterization and decoding benchmarks using circuit-level simulated syndromes yield a submillisecond post-exposure processing latency for selected small-code workloads ($d = 3, 5, 7$). By enabling logical blocks to be decoded before full-frame readout is complete, the architecture implements low-latency syndrome decoding, realizing real-time quantum information processing as required for fault-tolerant computation in atom arrays.

title: Dissipaton-embedded quantum master equation for nonlinear system-bath coupling
authors: Zi-Fan Zhu, Yao Wang, Rui-Xue Xu, YiJing Yan
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15198v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The dissipaton theory was proposed more than a decade ago as a statistical quasiparticle theory for open quantum systems and was soon extended to nonlinear system-bath coupling. Although numerical results provided strong evidence for its validity, a rigorous mathematical foundation, particularly for nonlinear system-bath coupling, was established only recently. On this basis, we formulate the dissipaton-embedded quantum master equation for nonlinear system-bath coupling. This in-principle exact master equation describes the joint dynamics of the reduced system and all dissipaton degrees of freedom.

title: Analytic T-Matrix Formalism for Helmholtz Resonators
authors: Egor V. Domoratskii, Polina A. Medvedeva, Dmitrii N. Maksimov, Lana A. Glazko, Alexey A. Proskurin, Nikolay S. Solodovchenko, Mingzhao Song, Yong Li, Mihail I. Petrov, Andrey A. Bogdanov
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15208v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We develop an analytic T-matrix formalism for two-dimensional circular acoustic Helmholtz resonators with thin rigid walls. The central idea is to use an aperture projection operator to obtain a compact expression for the T-matrix with explicit coefficients describing coupling and decoupling between external fields and cavity resonances. An equivalent formulation providing much faster convergence uses an aperture-to-Fourier map and an edge-adapted basis for the aperture flux. The method extends directly to multiple apertures of arbitrary angular widths and positions. The calculated scattering spectra agree with full-wave numerical simulations. For single- and double-aperture resonators, we decompose the T-matrix into even and odd parts under inversion to identify the channels associated with Willis coupling. We show how internal losses enable direction-dependent scattering and absorption when inversion symmetry is broken, while reciprocity ensures equal extinction for opposite incidence. Finally, we show how shifting the expansion origin redistributes radiation among multipole channels, enabling more compact T-matrix representations.

title: Trading Memory for Depth: Tight Bounds for LCU Block-Encodings
authors: Sebastian Issel
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15229v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: An LCU block-encoding of $A=\sum_j\alpha_j U_j$ runs the $U_j$ in series on one register, so its select depth is the total work $\sum_j d_j$. Depth was the one block-encoding constraint with no knob: grouping the $T$ terms into $g$ registers that run in parallel gives it one, and the binning is the knob. For a $g$-branched realisation (up to $g$ oracles in parallel) the select depth is tight at $\Theta(C+\log(g\,\max\{n,m\}))$ for $g\ge2$, with $C$ the binning makespan and $m$ the largest bin, in the $k$-local atomic-oracle model. The work floor is a two-way reduction to classical multiprocessor scheduling: every realisation \emph{induces} a $g$-machine schedule, and the construction realises any binning, so an optimal binning attains it. The additive logarithmic routing term is a light-cone cost, independent of the selector encoding and robust to register reuse, measurement, reset, and teleportation; width is at least $gn$. The standard $1/\alpha$ subnormalisation and success probability are unchanged; the endpoints are sequential LCU ($g{=}1$) and the fully parallel realisation ($g{=}T$). Allowing the oracles to be split (McNaughton's rule) reaches the work floor $\sum_j d_j/g$. Two selector realisations trade space for depth: a dense (M\"ott\"onen) one is memory-tight at the standard LCU footprint but its multiplexed controls cost a $\log\log(m{+}1)$ factor on the makespan; a one-hot one is depth-tight at $T$ selector qubits. Neither reaches both at once.

title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
authors: Maforikan Amoussou, Borja Aizpurua, Sukhbinder Singh, Rom\'an Or\'us, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15250v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.

title: Device-independent witnesses of genuine multipartite entanglement and nonlocality for GHZ states and Bell-pair tree
authors: Josep Batle, Tomasz Bia{\l}ecki, Adam Bednorz
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15283v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We derive and compare device-independent witnesses of genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) and genuine multipartite nonlocality (GMNL) for GHZ states and trees of Bell pairs. A binary-outcome family using four global measurement contexts has the tight biseparable bound independent of the number of parties. We distinguish these GME bounds from Svetlichny-hybrid bounds, which permit arbitrary communication within either side of a bipartition. For GHZ states, we also give a $2N$-context GMNL witness and compare it with MABK and Svetlichny tests. For Bell-pair trees, sums of CHSH and chained inequalities certify GME and GMNL, respectively, with explicitly specified input protocols and multi-bit local outputs. Separately, we prove the sharp four-context network bound $I_\lambda\leq2$ for every $N\geq3$ and $\lambda\geq2$, and bound the MABK scores of quantum networks assembled from bipartite sources. We successfully benchmark MABK, four-context, and Svetlichny witnesses on IBM Quantum GHZ preparations up to $10$ parties, under the local-measurement and sampling assumptions.

title: Quantum Recurrent Architectures for Financial Time Series Prediction
authors: Danyal Maheshwari, Gerhard Hellstern, Martin Zaefferer, Martin Braun, Tanja D\"ohler
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15298v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study evaluates quantum classical hybrid recurrent architectures for financial time-series forecasting: a Quantum Long Short-Term Memory (QLSTM) network and Quantum Reservoir Computing (QRC) with lag-based inputs. Classical lag vectors are encoded into quantum states via amplitude encoding, which compactly represents normalized observations but requires nontrivial state preparation; the QLSTM gates and the QRC reservoir are implemented with parameterized quantum circuits, while classical optimizers train the interface and readout layers. On a monthly revenue series extended to 1056 months by a Gaussian-process--hidden-Markov generator, with a fixed chronological 70/15/15 split and one-step-ahead forecasts, we compare both models against a full-size LSTM, a classical control matched in parameter budget and interface architecture, a small plain LSTM, and classical reservoir computing, over ten seeds and against persistence, seasonal-naive and SARIMA benchmark forecasts. The QLSTM, with 2,105 parameters, is statistically indistinguishable from an LSTM 126 times larger, but equally indistinguishable from the matched classical control and from a plain LSTM of the same budget, so its parameter efficiency cannot be attributed to the quantum circuits. The quantum reservoir is worse than a classical reservoir of equal feature dimension in all ten seeds and worse than SARIMA, whereas all recurrent models and both classical reservoirs improve on SARIMA by about 2\% in RMSE. In a 24-month rolling-origin backtest the classical LSTMs degrade more slowly than the QLSTM. We find no evidence of a quantum accuracy or parameter-efficiency advantage in this low-dimensional setting.

title: Cumulants of Operator Semigroups for Hierarchies of Many-Particle Evolution Equations
authors: V. I. Gerasimenko
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15304v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The paper presents a brief overview of recent advances in the mathematical theory of evolution equations for quantum many-particle systems.
  The structure of expansions representing non-perturbative solutions to the Cauchy problem for hierarchies of fundamental evolution equations for many quantum particles is outlined. It has been shown that the concept of cumulants of operator semigroups forms the basis for non-perturbative representation of solutions to hierarchies of evolution equations that describe the state and observables.
  It is proven that the constructed dynamics of correlations underlie the description of the evolution of the state, both for finitely and infinitely many particles, governed by the BBGKY hierarchy for reduced density operators or by the hierarchy of nonlinear evolution equations for reduced correlation operators. In fact, it is demonstrated that the behavior of particle correlations governs the dynamics of states in quantum systems with an infinite number of particles.

title: On the domain of the effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in quantum markovian dynamics
authors: Franco Fagnola, Zheng Li
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15322v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The GKLS representation of the unbounded generator of a quantum Markov semigroup crucially depends on an unbounded operator $G$, generating a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on the underlying Hilbert space, which is formally the sum of a negative self-adjoint operator $G_0$ and $-\mathrm{i}H$ with $H$ symmetric.
  In many situations it is useful to know the relationships between the domains of the three operators, in particular whether $\Dom(G)=\Dom(G_0)\cap\Dom(H)$ when both $G_0$ and $H$ are unbounded. In this note we show that this happens when $G_0$ and $H$ are self-adjoint quadratic polynomials in annihilation and creation operators in a finite-mode bosonic Fock space and $G_0\leq0$ or assuming a certain half bound on the commutator of $G_0$ and $H$.
  A counterexample shows that the conclusion does not hold in general situations.

title: Hybrid Classical-Quantum Optimization for CVRPTW: A Systems Framework with Provable Feasibility and Empirical Hardware Limits
authors: Syamasundar Gopasana, Swatantra Singh, Rohan Joydhar, Shubhashis Sengupta
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15343v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Solving large-scale Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problems with Time Windows (CVRPTW) remains challenging because strict operational constraints and scale limit both exact and heuristic methods. We present a hybrid classical-quantum architecture combining Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) with vehicle-level Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO), solved using Toshiba SQBM+ and QAOA on Rigetti Ankaa-3 and IQM Emerald quantum processors. The decomposition avoids the variable growth and constraint-enforcement difficulties of monolithic CVRPTW QUBO formulations. We evaluate the framework on five realistic benchmarks derived from London traffic and location data, spanning 10--70 customers, using a validation pipeline enforcing feasibility and monotone improvement over classical baselines. SQBM+ achieves verified fleet-distance reductions of 2.80% (7,927 m) for the 25-customer instance and 0.22% (1,186 m) for the 55-customer instance. QAOA experiments establish a current hardware boundary for reliable constraint satisfaction at subproblems of up to 4 customers (16 qubits). Diagnostic results identify assignment-level time-window tightness, rather than local route optimization, as the dominant scalability bottleneck. The results demonstrate a practical near-term role for hybrid classical-quantum optimization while establishing empirical limits for current quantum hardware.

title: On the statistical reliability of chaotic simulations at reduced precision
authors: Ross Ah-Weng, Peter V. Coveney
abstract:
arXiv:2611.15344v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reduced-precision arithmetic is increasingly used to accelerate scientific simulation, while AI workloads are driving its growing prominence in hardware design. Yet small arithmetic errors do not necessarily imply accurate statistics. Finite representation limits spatial resolution, while rounding can merge trajectories that should separate in chaotic systems, progressively concentrating probability on a shrinking collection of computer states. This redistribution can distort statistical averages well before periodicity becomes apparent; furthermore, disjoint computational basins can induce an initialisation bias, even when the intended equilibrium statistics are independent of the initial ensemble. We use functional graphs and their transfer operators to connect these pathologies to bounds on statistical bias, the duration of accurate averaging, and the effect of reducing precision. Exhaustive numerical experiments on four chaotic maps, with 1-24 significand bits and the 24-bit endpoint matching IEEE FP32, show how initially accurate ensembles drift towards incorrect statistics, with lower precision often bringing this deterioration forward. Stochastic rounding substantially extends some useful averaging windows but leaves others severely biased. Longer computed trajectories can therefore worsen inferred statistics, and a finite average can outperform the "infinite-time" computer average by orders of magnitude. This exposes a risk of statistically biased inference at reduced precision and provides a further motivation for collecting statistics from ensembles of shorter trajectories.
